messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
# Rajesh's Silence

Rajesh Patel was forty-nine years old when he first came to the clinic, though his wife said he looked older—that the light had gone out of him three years ago and had not returned. He had served as a medic in the Army for twenty-two years, had treated wounds in two deployments, had built a reputation for steadiness under pressure. But the injury that broke him came not in a combat zone but in his own home, inflicted by the person he had married.

The night it happened, Rajesh had come home late from his shift at the VA clinic where he worked now, retired from active duty. His husband Marcus was waiting in the kitchen, drunk, furious about something Rajesh could not quite parse through the slurred accusations. What began as argument became physical—Marcus's fists, his weight, the smell of his sweat and whiskey filling the small space as he drove Rajesh against the counter, into the wall. Rajesh, trained to protect others, could not protect himself. He did not fight back. When it was over, Marcus wept and apologized. Rajesh sat in the dark bathroom, cataloguing his injuries the way he had learned to do with soldiers: two fractured ribs, contusions across his shoulders and back, a split lip. The clinical inventory did nothing to contain what had happened.

Marcus promised it would never happen again. It did, three more times over the next eighteen months, each incident preceded by the same escalating tension, the same smell, the same feeling of being trapped in his own body. The last time, Marcus had driven his fist into Rajesh's lower back, and for weeks afterward Rajesh felt phantom pain in that exact spot whenever the memory surfaced—a sharp, electric ache that made him grip whatever was nearest to him. He had never reported any of it. The shame was too large. The fact that he had let it happen, that he had not left, that he had returned to the same house night after night, convinced him that there was something fundamentally broken in him, some defect that made him deserve what was happening.

By the time Marcus finally left him—not because Rajesh asked him to, but because Marcus met someone else—the damage had already calcified into habit. Rajesh had begun to avoid the clothes he had worn during those years: the khaki work shirts he favored, the loose cotton pants. He bought smaller sizes, tighter cuts, as if shedding the old silhouette might shed the memory. He stopped going to the gym, where he had lifted weights for thirty years. The thought of being in a contained space, surrounded by other bodies, the smell of sweat in the air—it made his chest tight. He told himself he was too busy, too tired, but the truth was that the gym had become a place where his body felt exposed, where he might encounter someone who smelled like Marcus, who moved like Marcus.

At work, his colleagues had noticed the change. Rajesh had always been the one who volunteered for extra shifts, who mentored the younger medics. Now he requested the quietest clinic hours, avoided the busy mornings when patients crowded the waiting room. His supervisor had gently asked if everything was all right. Rajesh had said yes, but they both knew it was a lie. He had become unreliable in small ways—missing meetings, requesting time off, flinching when someone approached him too quickly. One resident had made a comment about how jumpy the old medic had become, and Rajesh had felt the shame flood through him again.

Sleep had become a battlefield. Rajesh would lie in bed, every muscle tensed, unable to let himself drift because the moment he did, he would be back in that kitchen, Marcus's breath on his neck, his own powerlessness absolute. He kept the lights on low all night. He had rearranged the bedroom so he could see the door. He had come to believe that the only place he was truly safe was his locked bedroom, and even there, the safety was fragile, dependent on vigilance he could not sustain forever.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a simple thing: a police officer had come to his door about a noise complaint from a neighbor. Rajesh had opened the door to find the uniform, the authority, the power imbalance, and he had felt the world tilt. He could not speak. His hands had begun to shake. The officer, confused and concerned, had asked if he was all right, and Rajesh had been unable to answer. That night, he had called his sister, who had insisted he see someone. He was terrified of what that meant—of having to speak about what had happened, of having to put into words something that lived in his body as sensation and silence. But he was more terrified of continuing to live the way he had been, trapped in the small circle of his bedroom, watching his career collapse, watching his wife watch him disappear. He came to the first appointment because he could no longer bear the alternative.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Relationship Status: Married (vignette describes husband Marcus, but also references 'wife' in opening, creating confusion about actual marital status and partner gender): CRITICAL DEMOGRAPHIC INCONSISTENCY: The vignette opens with 'his wife said he looked older' but then reveals the abuser is 'his husband Marcus.' The patient's reported relationship status is 'Married' but the vignette creates ambiguity about whether Rajesh is married to Marcus (the abuser, now departed) or to a wife. This is a fundamental demographic contradiction that undermines the vignette's accuracy. Additionally, the patient is described as having a 'wife' in the opening, but the trauma involves abuse by 'husband Marcus'—this is inconsistent with the stated trauma type of 'Physical abuse by romantic partner' and creates confusion about the patient's actual relationship configuration and current marital status.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

Rajesh Patel was forty-nine years old when he first came to the clinic, though his husband Vikram said he looked older—that the light had gone out of him three years ago and had not returned. Rajesh had served as a medic in the Army for twenty-two years, had treated wounds in two deployments, had built a reputation for steadiness under pressure. But the injury that broke him came not in a combat zone but in his own home, inflicted by the person he had married before that life began. The night it happened, Rajesh had come home late from his shift at the VA clinic where he worked now, retired from active duty. His ex-husband Marcus was waiting in the kitchen, drunk, furious about something Rajesh could not quite parse through the slurred accusations. What began as argument became physical—Marcus's fists, his weight, the smell of his sweat and whiskey filling the small space as he drove Rajesh against the counter, into the wall. Rajesh, trained to protect others, could not protect himself. He did not fight back. When it was over, Marcus wept and apologized. Rajesh sat in the dark bathroom, cataloguing his injuries the way he had learned to do with soldiers: two fractured ribs, contusions across his shoulders and back, a split lip. The clinical inventory did nothing to contain what had happened.

Marcus promised it would never happen again. It did, three more times over the next eighteen months, each incident preceded by the same escalating tension, the same smell, the same feeling of being trapped in his own body. The last time, Marcus had driven his fist into Rajesh's lower back, and for weeks afterward Rajesh felt phantom pain in that exact spot whenever the memory surfaced—a sharp, electric ache that made him grip whatever was nearest to him. He had never reported any of it. The shame was too large. The fact that he had let it happen, that he had not left, that he had returned to the same house night after night, convinced him that there was something fundamentally broken in him, some defect that made him deserve what was happening. When Marcus finally left him—not because Rajesh asked him to, but because Marcus met someone else—the damage had already calcified into habit. By then, Rajesh had been separated from Marcus for two years, had rebuilt a quiet life with Vikram, a man who had never raised his voice, who made tea in the morning and asked how Rajesh had slept. But the past had not released him.

Rajesh had begun to avoid the clothes he had worn during those years: the khaki work shirts he favored, the loose cotton pants. He bought smaller sizes, tighter cuts, as if shedding the old silhouette might shed the memory. He stopped going to the gym, where he had lifted weights for thirty years. The thought of being in a contained space, surrounded by other bodies, the smell of sweat in the air—it made his chest tight. He told himself he was too busy, too tired, but the truth was that the gym had become a place where his body felt exposed, where he might encounter someone who smelled like Marcus, who moved like Marcus. At work, his colleagues had noticed the change. Rajesh had always been the one who volunteered for extra shifts, who mentored the younger medics. Now he requested the quietest clinic hours, avoided the busy mornings when patients crowded the waiting room. His supervisor had gently asked if everything was all right. Rajesh had said yes, but they both knew it was a lie. He had become unreliable in small ways—missing meetings, requesting time off, flinching when someone approached him too quickly. One resident had made a comment about how jumpy the old medic had become, and Rajesh had felt the shame flood through him again. Vikram had noticed too. He had asked, several times, why Rajesh seemed distant, why he no longer wanted to go out, why he insisted on keeping the bedroom door locked even when they were home together. Rajesh could not explain it without saying the words, and the words felt impossible.

Sleep had become a battlefield. Rajesh would lie in bed, every muscle tensed, unable to let himself drift because the moment he did, he would be back in that kitchen, Marcus's breath on his neck, his own powerlessness absolute. He kept the lights on low all night. He had rearranged the bedroom so he could see the door. He had come to believe that the only place he was truly safe was his locked bedroom, and even there, the safety was fragile, dependent on vigilance he could not sustain forever. Vikram had begun to sleep in the guest room, hurt and confused by the rejection. What finally brought Rajesh to the clinic was a simple thing: a police officer had come to his door about a noise complaint from a neighbor. Rajesh had opened the door to find the uniform, the authority, the power imbalance, and he had felt the world tilt. He could not speak. His hands had begun to shake. The officer, confused and concerned, had asked if he was all right, and Rajesh had been unable to answer. That night, he had called his sister, who had insisted he see someone. He was terrified of what that meant—of having to speak about what had happened, of having to put into words something that lived in his body as sensation and silence. But he was more terrified of continuing to live the way he had been, watching his marriage to Vikram hollow out from the inside, watching his career collapse, trapped in the small circle of his bedroom with the door locked against a danger that had already left. He came to the first appointment because he could no longer bear the alternative.
